title: Lines, characters and jumps
summary: Jump within a line with 0 ^ $ f t ; , and across the file with gg G :n % { }.

steps.title: Within a line
body: | `f` + char | next occurrence of that char on the line |
| `,` | repeat it in the opposite direction |
`f` is the fastest way to reach a spot you can see: look at the character, type `f` and it.
> **Practise:** open **Labs → Vim & nano trainer** and run this lesson's challenges until the keys come without thinking.

steps.prompt: The line is `    return x + y;` (four leading spaces) and the cursor is on the `x`. You press `^`. Which character is the cursor on?
steps.explain: `^` goes to the first non-blank character; `0` would go to the very first column (a space).

steps.prompt: The line is `a,b,c,d` with the cursor on `a`. You press `f,` then `;` then `;`. Which letter comes right after the cursor's comma?
steps.explain: `f,` reaches the first comma, each `;` the next: three commas in, the cursor is on the comma before `d`.

steps.prompt: The line is `name = "value"` with the cursor on `n`. Which keys put the cursor on the `e` that ends `value`?
steps.explain: `$` reaches the closing quote and `h` steps back one. Three `e`s stop at `name`, `=`, then the opening quote; two `f"` land on the closing quote.

steps.title: Across the file
body: | `H` `M` `L` | top / middle / bottom of the screen |
| `Ctrl+O` | back to where you were before the last jump |
`%` is a lifesaver in code and JSON: put the cursor on a brace and jump to its partner. If the cursor is not on a bracket, `%` uses the first one to the right on the line.

steps.prompt: Match the keys to the jump.
Go to the first line, then jump to the brace that matches the one at the end of that line.
steps.explain: `gg` first line, `$` to its last character (the `{`), `%` to the matching `}`.

steps.title: Motions in real Vim: strip trailing comments
prompt: `~/servers.conf` has comments at the end of some lines. Remove each trailing comment **and the spaces before it**. Lines that are only a comment (starting with `#`) stay as they are.

Motions are not only for moving: `:normal` runs Normal-mode keys on every line of a range, so `:%norm f#D` means "on each line, jump to the next `#` and delete to the end". If a motion fails on a line (no `#` after the cursor), Vim stops the keys **for that line only**, which is exactly what you want for the full-line comments: the cursor starts on their `#`, and `f#` looks only to the right.
This terminal runs Vim's command line without the screen: `vim -es -c 'cmd1' -c 'cmd2' -c x file` (`x` writes and quits).
One `:normal` command can do it all if you find the motion that lands on the space before `#`; two commands (`:normal` then a `:s` for the trailing spaces) are fine too.

checks.name: trailing comments and their spaces are gone, full-line comments stay
checks.fail: `~/servers.conf` is not right yet. The diff below shows what still differs (`<` is the goal, `>` is your file). Trailing spaces count: `cat -A` shows them as spaces before `$`.

checks.name: no Vim is left running
checks.fail: A Vim process is still waiting for commands. Type `q!` and Enter in it, or `pkill vim`.

hints: `f#` jumps to the next `#` on the line; `D` deletes from the cursor to the end of the line. `:%norm f#D` does that on every line.

That leaves the spaces before the old comment. Remove them with `:%s/\s\+$//e` (the `e` flag means "no error if nothing matches"). Or use `ge` (end of the previous word) and `l` to land on the first space.
`vim -es -c '%norm f#D' -c '%s/\s\+$//e' -c x ~/servers.conf` or, in one go, `vim -es -c '%norm f#gelD' -c x ~/servers.conf`.
steps.explain: `f#` then `ge` (back to the end of the previous word) then `l` lands on the first space, and `D` deletes from there to the end. On full-line comments `f#` finds nothing to the right of the cursor, so Vim skips the rest of the keys for that line. Failing motions stopping a key sequence is also how macros know when to stop.
